history: Une tasse first appears in French among a prince's treasures. The TLFi traces it to Arabic ṭāsa or ṭassa, a cup or bowl, which Arabic had taken from Persian tašt. Spanish had taza by 1272, Provençal tassa by 1344, and Italian tazza in the 14th century; French most probably took the word from Provençal or Italian. Its first French appearance is in an inventory of the jewels of Louis, Duke of Anjou, written between 1360 and 1368, where it is a precious drinking vessel. Today the word is as everyday as it gets: une tasse de café, une tasse de thé. And if you swallow water by accident while swimming, the French say you boire la tasse, ‘drink the cup’.
historyEinfach: Tasse comes from Arabic ṭāsa, ‘cup’. The Arabs took it from Persian. The word came to French through Provençal or Italian. Spanish says taza and Italian tazza. In French: une tasse de café, ‘a cup of coffee’.

elsewhere.text: Spanish had the word before French did, by 1272: the Arabic of al-Andalus was close at hand.
